mainEntity.name: What is the difference between LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: LocalDate represents a date only (year-month-day) with no time or time zone — perfect for birthdays, holidays, and deadlines. LocalDateTime represents a date AND time (year-month-day-hour-minute-second) but with no time zone — useful for scheduling within one zone. ZonedDateTime represents a date, time, AND time zone — the complete temporal value for cross-timezone operations, meeting scheduling, and anything that needs to represent a precise global moment. Rule of thumb: use the simplest type that carries the information you actually need.

mainEntity.name: What is wrong with java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar?

acceptedAnswer.text: java.util.Date has multiple design flaws: (1) Mutable — not thread-safe. (2) January is month 0 — off-by-one errors everywhere. (3) Year is stored as (year - 1900) — getYear() returns 124 for 2024. (4) Despite the name, it represents both date AND time (milliseconds since epoch). (5) No time zone support. (6) Most methods are deprecated. Calendar is even more verbose and error-prone. Java 8's java.time package (based on Joda-Time) replaced both entirely with an immutable, fluent, thread-safe API.

Instant represents a specific point on the global timeline — nanoseconds elapsed since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC). It is time zone-independent, always in UTC, and the most precise temporal type in java.time. Use Instant for: timestamping events, database timestamp columns, measuring elapsed time (with Duration), logging, and any operation that needs a precise machine-readable moment. Convert to human-readable form using atZone(ZoneId) when display is needed.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Duration and Period in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Duration measures time in machine units — seconds and nanoseconds. It is used with time-based values: LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Instant. Example: Duration between two LocalDateTime instances. Period measures time in calendar units — years, months, days. It is used with date-only values: LocalDate. Example: Period between two LocalDates. Key insight: Duration.ofDays(1) is always exactly 86,400 seconds, but Period.ofDays(1) is 'one calendar day' which may be 23 or 25 hours during Daylight Saving Time transitions.

mainEntity.name: How do you format a date in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use DateTimeFormatter from java.time.format. Two approaches: (1) Predefined formats: DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE, DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE_TIME, etc. (2) Custom pattern: DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd-MMM-yyyy HH:mm:ss'). Formatting: String formatted = localDate.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd/MM/yyyy')). Parsing: LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse('25/12/2026', DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd/MM/yyyy')). DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe and can be stored as a static final constant. Never use the old, thread-unsafe SimpleDateFormat in new code.

articleHeader.title: Java Date & Time — LocalDate, ZonedDateTime, Formatting & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete guide to Java Date & Time — from the broken legacy API to the modern java.time package. Covers LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Instant, Duration, Period, DateTimeFormatter, TemporalAdjusters, DST pitfalls, and production-ready patterns.

sections.title: A Brief History of Java Date APIs — Three Generations

blocks.text: Java's date and time handling has a famously troubled history — spanning three distinct generations over 25+ years. Understanding why the API evolved the way it did is essential context for every Java developer: it explains why the codebase you maintain might be using three different date APIs simultaneously, and it makes the design decisions of java.time immediately clear.

items.title: Generation 1 — java.util.Date (Java 1.0, 1995)
items.text: The original java.util.Date was designed in haste and is widely regarded as one of Java's worst design decisions. It is mutable (not thread-safe), months are 0-indexed (January = 0), years are stored as (year - 1900), and despite being named 'Date' it also stores time. Most of its methods were deprecated in Java 1.1. Still found in legacy codebases and some JDBC APIs.

items.title: Generation 2 — java.util.Calendar (Java 1.1, 1997)
items.text: Calendar was introduced to fix Date's problems. It partially succeeded — it added time zone support and fixed the year storage issue — but it remained mutable, was even more verbose, still used 0-indexed months, and mixed date/time concepts in one bloated class. Calendar arithmetic was notoriously error-prone. The community turned to Joda-Time, a third-party library, as the de-facto standard.

items.title: Generation 3 — java.time (Java 8, 2014, JSR-310)
items.text: java.time was designed by the author of Joda-Time (Stephen Colebourne) as JSR-310 and is a ground-up redesign. Key principles: immutability (all types are thread-safe), clear separation of concepts (date-only, time-only, with-zone, machine-time), fluent API, nanosecond precision, and comprehensive time zone support via the IANA timezone database. This is the only API you should use in new code written after Java 8.

blocks.title: 📌 Which API Should You Use in 2026?
blocks.text: New code: exclusively java.time (java.time.LocalDate, java.time.ZonedDateTime, etc.). Legacy code using java.util.Date or Calendar: migrate to java.time — bridge methods like Date.toInstant() and Calendar.toInstant() exist for this. Third-party: Joda-Time is still maintained but its author explicitly says 'Migrate to java.time; it is essentially the same design.' Never use SimpleDateFormat in new code — use DateTimeFormatter.

sections.title: Legacy API: java.util.Date & Calendar — The Problems You Must Know

blocks.text: Even if you never write new legacy Date code, you will encounter it in production codebases, third-party libraries, and JDBC results. Understanding its specific failure modes prevents subtle bugs during maintenance — and explains every interview question about why java.util.Date was replaced.

cal.set(2026, Calendar.MARCH, 20); // Correct way — use constants
Date d = new Date(2026 - 1900, 2, 20); // Deprecated constructor
// ❌ PROBLEM 4: Date also stores time (misleading name)
Date today = new Date(); // Has hours, minutes, seconds, millis too
// 'Date' is really a 'DateAndTime' — milliseconds since Unix epoch
// ❌ PROBLEM 5: No time zone in java.util.Date

// What about 'same day regardless of time'? No built-in way.

blocks.title: ⚠️ The SimpleDateFormat Thread-Safety Trap
blocks.text: SimpleDateFormat is stateful and NOT thread-safe. A notorious production bug: storing a static SimpleDateFormat in a shared service class and calling format()/parse() from multiple threads — leads to corrupted output, wrong dates, and impossible-to-reproduce bugs. Fix: either create a new SimpleDateFormat instance per call (expensive), use ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>, or better yet — migrate to DateTimeFormatter, which IS thread-safe and can be safely shared as static final.

sections.title: java.time Package — Architecture & Core Types

blocks.text: The java.time package (introduced in Java 8 as JSR-310) organises date/time concepts into a clear taxonomy. Every type is immutable and thread-safe. Every modification method (like plusDays() or withMonth()) returns a new instance — the original is never modified. The API is fluent — methods return the same type, enabling clean method chaining.

blocks.title: 💡 The Golden Rule for Choosing the Right Type
blocks.text: Ask yourself three questions: (1) Do I need a DATE or a TIME or BOTH? → LocalDate / LocalTime / LocalDateTime. (2) Do I need to handle multiple time zones or precise global moments? → ZonedDateTime (for human use) or Instant (for machine use). (3) Am I measuring a SPAN of time? → Duration (for time-based) or Period (for calendar-based). The simplest type that accurately models your requirement is always the right choice.

sections.title: LocalDate — Date Without Time or Zone

blocks.text: LocalDate represents a date — year, month, day — with no time component and no time zone. It is the right choice for any domain concept that is inherently date-only: a person's birthday, a public holiday, a project deadline, a payment due date. Internally, LocalDate stores year (int), month (Month enum), and day (int). It is immutable and thread-safe.

blocks.label: LocalDateDemo.java
lines: LocalDate withEnum = LocalDate.of(2026, Month.AUGUST, 15); // Same, using enum
boolean isBusinessDay = dow != DayOfWeek.SATURDAY && dow != DayOfWeek.SUNDAY;

blocks.title: 💡 Month is 1-Indexed in java.time — No More January=0 Bug!
blocks.text: One of java.time's most celebrated fixes: months are 1-indexed. January = 1, December = 12. LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 26) is January 26 — exactly as you'd expect. The old Calendar.JANUARY = 0 bug that caused countless production incidents is gone. You can also use the Month enum for maximum clarity: LocalDate.of(2026, Month.JANUARY, 26). Both approaches are readable and correct.

sections.title: LocalTime — Time Without Date or Zone

blocks.text: LocalTime represents a time of day — hour, minute, second, nanosecond — with no date and no time zone. It models the wall-clock time seen on a clock face, independent of any particular day. Perfect for representing store opening hours, shift schedules, alarm times, and daily recurring events that are not tied to a specific calendar date.

sections.title: LocalDateTime — Date and Time, No Zone

blocks.text: LocalDateTime is the combination of LocalDate and LocalTime — it holds a date AND time with no time zone information. It is ideal for recording timestamps within a single time zone context, like a meeting scheduled at a specific date and time within one region, or a database timestamp column where the application always operates in one known time zone.

sections.title: ZonedDateTime — The Complete Temporal Type

blocks.text: ZonedDateTime is the most complete temporal type in java.time — it stores a date, time, UTC offset, AND time zone ID. Unlike LocalDateTime, it unambiguously identifies a precise point in time visible to a person in a specific region. It correctly handles Daylight Saving Time (DST) transitions, historical time zone changes, and cross-timezone arithmetic. Use it when your application genuinely needs to reason about time in multiple zones.

blocks.title: ⚠️ withZoneSameInstant() vs withZoneSameLocal() — Critical Distinction
blocks.text: withZoneSameInstant(zone) converts the same MOMENT to another zone — like asking 'what does a clock in Kolkata show right now?' The underlying instant (epoch millis) doesn't change. withZoneSameLocal(zone) keeps the CLOCK READING the same but changes the zone — creating a DIFFERENT instant. Example: 10:00 AM New York → withZoneSameInstant(Kolkata) = 19:30 IST (same moment). 10:00 AM New York → withZoneSameLocal(Kolkata) = 10:00 IST (different moment — 9.5 hours earlier). Mixing these up causes ghost meeting bugs.

sections.title: Instant — The Machine Timestamp

blocks.text: Instant represents a single, specific point on the global timeline — the number of seconds (and nanoseconds) elapsed since the Unix epoch: January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC. It has no time zone, no DST consideration, no calendar system — it is the rawest, most machine-centric time value in java.time. Instant is the go-to type for event timestamping, database records, elapsed time measurement, and logging.

Instant future = Instant.now().plusSeconds(3600); // 1 hour from now

blocks.title: 📌 Instant vs ZonedDateTime — When to Use Which
blocks.text: Instant is for MACHINES — storing when something happened (database created_at, audit log timestamp, JWT iat claim). It has no zone, no DST, no ambiguity. ZonedDateTime is for HUMANS — displaying when something happens to a person in a specific locale. Rule: store as Instant (or OffsetDateTime for SQL), display as ZonedDateTime. Never store ZonedDateTime in a database — the zone info is presentation logic, not data. Store epoch seconds or UTC timestamps.

sections.title: Duration vs Period — Measuring Time Gaps Correctly

blocks.text: Java provides two distinct types for representing an amount of time: Duration for machine-precision time spans, and Period for human-calendar spans. Choosing the wrong one leads to subtle DST-related bugs — one of the most insidious classes of datetime errors in production systems.

sections.title: DateTimeFormatter — Formatting & Parsing

blocks.text: DateTimeFormatter is the thread-safe, immutable replacement for SimpleDateFormat. It converts between java.time objects and String in both directions: formatting (date object → string) and parsing (string → date object). It supports predefined ISO patterns, custom patterns, locale-sensitive formats, and even optional sections.

items.title: Predefined ISO Formatters
items.text: DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE → '2026-08-15'. ISO_LOCAL_TIME → '10:30:00'. ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME → '2026-08-15T10:30:00'. ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME → '2026-08-15T10:30:00+05:30'. ISO_INSTANT → '2026-08-15T05:00:00Z'. ISO_ZONED_DATE_TIME → '2026-08-15T10:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata]'. These are the defaults used by toString() on java.time objects.

items.title: Pattern Letters — Custom Formats
items.text: y=year, M=month, d=day, H=hour(0-23), h=hour(1-12), m=minute, s=second, n=nanosecond, a=AM/PM, z=zone name, Z=zone offset, E=day name, D=day of year, w=week of year. Case and repetition matter: M=month digit, MM=zero-padded, MMM=Jan, MMMM=January. H=hour, HH=zero-padded. Always quote literal text with single quotes: 'T' in a pattern is literal T.

items.title: Locale-Sensitive Formatters
items.text: DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.FULL) produces locale-aware output. With Locale.of('hi', 'IN') you get Hindi format; with Locale.US you get US format. FormatStyle options: FULL ('Thursday, March 20, 2026'), LONG ('March 20, 2026'), MEDIUM ('Mar 20, 2026'), SHORT ('3/20/26'). Use withLocale(Locale) to chain: DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.LONG).withLocale(Locale.UK).

items.title: Thread Safety — Static Constants Are Safe
items.text: Unlike SimpleDateFormat, DateTimeFormatter is IMMUTABLE and THREAD-SAFE. Store it safely as a private static final field: private static final DateTimeFormatter INDIAN_FORMAT = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd-MMM-yyyy'); This is the standard pattern in production code — create once, reuse everywhere, no synchronization needed.

sections.title: TemporalAdjusters — Navigating the Calendar Like a Pro

blocks.text: TemporalAdjusters is a utility class in java.time.temporal providing factory methods for common calendar navigation tasks — finding the next Monday, the last day of the month, the second Tuesday of the month, and so on. These cover the kinds of date calculations that plague financial, HR, and scheduling systems — calculations that look simple but have dozens of edge cases.

sections.title: ChronoUnit — Measuring Between Dates with Precision

blocks.text: ChronoUnit is an enum in java.time.temporal representing standard units of time — from nanoseconds to millennia. Its most practical method is between(temporal1, temporal2), which calculates the number of complete units between two temporal objects. It is the clearest way to answer questions like: 'How many days until the deadline?' or 'How many months has this subscription been active?'

sections.title: Time Zone Handling & DST Pitfalls — The Hard Part

blocks.text: Time zones are the most complex part of any date/time system. The IANA Time Zone Database (also called the tz or zoneinfo database) is Java's source of truth — accessed via ZoneId. It defines over 600 named zones, each with its complete history of UTC offsets and DST transitions. Getting time zones right in production requires understanding three common failure modes: DST gaps, DST overlaps, and offset vs zone ID.

blocks.label: TimeZoneHandling.java
lines: // ✅ ZoneId vs ZoneOffset — know the difference
ZoneId    kolkataZoneId = ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata");    // Named zone — full DST history
ZoneOffset fixedOffset  = ZoneOffset.of("+05:30");       // Fixed offset — no DST logic
ZoneOffset utcOffset    = ZoneOffset.UTC;                // UTC — zero offset
// India doesn't observe DST — so both are equivalent for IST
// But for America/New_York (which does DST), they behave differently:
// ✅ DST GAP — 'Spring Forward': an hour that doesn't exist
// US Eastern DST starts: 2026-03-08 02:00 → jumps to 03:00
// So 02:30 AM on March 8 does NOT EXIST in America/New_York
// ✅ DST OVERLAP — 'Fall Back': an hour that appears twice
// US Eastern DST ends: 2026-11-01 02:00 → falls back to 01:00
// So 01:30 AM on Nov 1 is AMBIGUOUS — could be -04:00 or -05:00
// ✅ Best practice: store as Instant, display in user's zone
Instant eventInstant = Instant.parse("2026-04-10T09:00:00Z"); // Stored in DB
DateTimeFormatter fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd MMM yyyy HH:mm z");
System.out.println("\nGlobal display of the same event:");

blocks.title: ⚠️ The 3 Most Dangerous Time Zone Mistakes in Production
blocks.text: 1. Storing ZonedDateTime as a string in the database (zone name gets lost on read). Fix: store as TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (SQL) mapped to OffsetDateTime (Java). 2. Using ZoneOffset.of('+05:30') instead of ZoneId.of('Asia/Kolkata') — the fixed offset never adjusts for DST or historical changes. 3. Using LocalDateTime.now() without specifying a zone — it uses the JVM's default zone, which varies by server. Fix: always pass the zone explicitly: LocalDateTime.now(ZoneId.of('Asia/Kolkata')).

blocks.text: If you work in any codebase more than a few years old, you will encounter java.util.Date, java.util.Calendar, and java.sql.Timestamp. Java provides official bridge methods on the legacy classes to convert to and from java.time types — enabling incremental migration without rewriting everything at once.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Causes Production Incidents

blocks.text: Date/time bugs are disproportionately responsible for production incidents — they are hard to reproduce (depend on the current time, JVM timezone, or DST state), silent (no exception, just wrong data), and costly (incorrect billing, missed deadlines, corrupted records). These are the most common anti-patterns found in enterprise Java codebases.

items.title: Using LocalDateTime for Cross-Timezone Operations
items.text: Scheduling a meeting at LocalDateTime.of(2026, 4, 10, 10, 0) and sending it to participants in different time zones is a silent bug. LocalDateTime has no zone — it cannot represent a global moment. Use ZonedDateTime or Instant for any event involving multiple time zones. The meeting in NYC at 10:00 AM is 19:30 IST — LocalDateTime captures neither correctly.

items.title: Relying on JVM Default Timezone
items.text: LocalDateTime.now() and ZonedDateTime.now() without an explicit ZoneId use ZoneId.systemDefault() — which varies between developer machines, CI servers, and production servers. A JVM arg change, Docker base image update, or server migration can silently shift all timestamps. Always be explicit: LocalDateTime.now(ZoneId.of('Asia/Kolkata')). Never assume the JVM's default zone.

items.title: Using SimpleDateFormat as a Shared Static Field
items.text: private static final SimpleDateFormat SDF = new SimpleDateFormat('dd/MM/yyyy') is a classic thread-safety bug. SimpleDateFormat uses internal state during format/parse — concurrent calls corrupt each other's output. Fix: use DateTimeFormatter (thread-safe), or create a new SimpleDateFormat per call, or use ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>.

items.title: Storing java.util.Date.getTime() as Business Data
items.text: Using epoch milliseconds (System.currentTimeMillis()) directly in business logic — storing them in databases, sending them in APIs, comparing them — makes your code opaque and error-prone. Use Instant, LocalDate, or ZonedDateTime which carry semantic meaning. When you see 1711929600000L you need to decode it; when you see 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z you understand it instantly.

items.title: Comparing Dates with == or Ignoring Time Component
items.text: new Date() == new Date() is always false (reference comparison). date1.equals(date2) compares millisecond precision — two 'same day' dates with different times won't be equal. For same-day comparison: date1.toLocalDate().isEqual(date2.toLocalDate()). For range checks: always use isBefore/isAfter on LocalDate or compareTo on Instant.

items.title: Ignoring DST During 'Add One Day' Operations
items.text: On DST transition days, adding 24 hours to a ZonedDateTime gives a different wall-clock time than 'tomorrow'. Use Period.ofDays(1) (calendar-aware) not Duration.ofDays(1) (exactly 86400 seconds) when you mean 'the same time tomorrow'. Example: adding Duration.ofDays(1) to 10:00 AM on the night clocks go forward gives 11:00 AM — not 10:00 AM as a user would expect.

sections.title: Java Date & Time Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are asked in Java developer interviews from junior to senior level, in Spring Boot technical rounds, and in backend architect assessments.

items.q: Q1. What are the main problems with java.util.Date and Calendar?
items.a: java.util.Date problems: (1) Mutable — not thread-safe. (2) January = 0 (months are 0-indexed) — causes widespread off-by-one bugs. (3) getYear() returns (year-1900) — 2026 returns 126. (4) Despite name 'Date', it stores both date AND time as milliseconds since epoch. (5) No time zone support built in. (6) Most methods deprecated in Java 1.1. Calendar problems: (1) Still mutable. (2) Still 0-indexed months. (3) Extremely verbose API — requires 5+ lines for simple operations. (4) No immutability or thread safety. Solution: java.time package (Java 8, JSR-310) replaces both entirely with an immutable, fluent, clear API.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime?
items.a: LocalDate: date only (2026-08-15) — no time, no zone. Use for birthdays, holidays, deadlines. LocalDateTime: date + time (2026-08-15T10:30:00) — no zone. Use for scheduling within one zone, DB timestamps where zone is implicit. ZonedDateTime: date + time + zone (2026-08-15T10:30:00+05:30[Asia/Kolkata]) — the complete temporal value. Use for cross-timezone events, flight schedules, global meeting planning. Design rule: use the simplest type that accurately models your requirement. Adding time zone when not needed creates complexity; omitting it when needed creates incorrect behaviour.

items.q: Q3. What is Instant and when should you use it instead of ZonedDateTime?
items.a: Instant represents a point on the global timeline — nanoseconds since Unix epoch (Jan 1, 1970 UTC). It has no zone, no DST, no calendar system. Use Instant for: (1) Database timestamps (created_at, updated_at) — store as TIMESTAMP/BIGINT, read as Instant. (2) Logging and audit trails — precise machine timestamps. (3) Measuring elapsed time: Duration.between(start, end). (4) JWT claims (iat, exp). (5) Message queue timestamps. Use ZonedDateTime for: presenting time to a human in their timezone, scheduling events users will see. Rule: store as Instant, display as ZonedDateTime. Instant is for machines; ZonedDateTime is for people.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between Duration and Period in Java?
items.a: Duration measures time in MACHINE units — seconds and nanoseconds. It is exact: Duration.ofDays(1) is always 86,400 seconds regardless of DST. Use with LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Instant. Period measures time in CALENDAR units — years, months, days. It is human-intuitive: Period.ofMonths(1) added to March 31 gives April 30 (not May 1). Use with LocalDate. The classic DST trap: adding Duration.ofDays(1) to a ZonedDateTime on a DST transition night may give 23 or 25 hours, not 24. Adding Period.ofDays(1) gives 'the same clock time tomorrow' — usually what users expect.

items.q: Q5. Why is SimpleDateFormat not thread-safe? What is the fix?
items.a: SimpleDateFormat maintains internal state (a Calendar instance) during format and parse operations. When two threads call format() or parse() concurrently on the same SimpleDateFormat instance, they corrupt each other's internal state — producing wrong dates, exceptions, or silent incorrect output. This is a non-deterministic, hard-to-reproduce race condition. Three fixes: (1) Best: use DateTimeFormatter (java.time.format) — it is immutable and thread-safe by design, safe as static final. (2) Acceptable: create a new SimpleDateFormat per method call (no sharing, but GC pressure). (3) Legacy workaround: ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> — one instance per thread.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between withZoneSameInstant() and withZoneSameLocal()?
items.a: withZoneSameInstant(zone) converts the same MOMENT (epoch millis unchanged) to another zone — like saying 'what does a clock in Kolkata read right now?' The wall-clock time changes; the underlying instant does not. withZoneSameLocal(zone) keeps the CLOCK READING the same but changes the zone — creating a different instant. Example: 10:00 AM New York EST (UTC-5). withZoneSameInstant(Asia/Kolkata) = 19:30 IST (same moment, different clock). withZoneSameLocal(Asia/Kolkata) = 10:00 IST (different moment — 10:00 Kolkata is 9.5 hours before 10:00 New York). Mixing them up causes meeting schedule bugs.

items.q: Q7. How do you calculate the number of days between two dates in Java?
items.a: Three correct approaches: (1) ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(startDate, endDate) — cleanest, returns long, works with LocalDate and LocalDateTime. (2) Period.between(startDate, endDate).getDays() — WRONG for total days! getDays() returns only the day component of the period, not total days. Period.between(Jan 1, Mar 20).getDays() returns 19 (days part of 2 months and 19 days), not 78 total days. (3) startDate.until(endDate, ChronoUnit.DAYS) — equivalent to option 1. Never use Date subtraction (date1.getTime() - date2.getTime()) / 86_400_000 — fails during DST transitions and leap seconds.

items.q: Q8. How do you store and retrieve dates in a JDBC/JPA application?
items.a: With JDBC 4.2+: Use LocalDate for DATE columns (setObject/getObject with LocalDate). Use LocalDateTime for DATETIME columns. Use OffsetDateTime or Instant for TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE columns. Never use java.sql.Date or java.sql.Timestamp in new code. With JPA/Hibernate 5+: annotate LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, and Instant fields directly — no @Temporal annotation needed. Hibernate handles the mapping. Best practice: store timestamps as TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (PostgreSQL) or DATETIME (MySQL, note: MySQL DATETIME has no zone) mapped to OffsetDateTime in Java. Store date-only values (birthdays) as LocalDate mapped to DATE column.

items.q: Q9. What is TemporalAdjuster and give a real-world example?
items.a: TemporalAdjuster is a functional interface that adjusts a temporal object to produce a new temporal. TemporalAdjusters (utility class) provides factory methods for calendar navigation. Real-world example: Indian payroll — salary is credited on the 25th of each month, but if the 25th falls on a Saturday or Sunday, it is credited on the preceding Friday. Implementation: LocalDate payday = YearMonth.now().atDay(25); if (payday.getDayOfWeek() == SATURDAY) payday = payday.minusDays(1); if (payday.getDayOfWeek() == SUNDAY) payday = payday.minusDays(2);. Or using a custom TemporalAdjuster: payday.with(date -> { DayOfWeek dow = LocalDate.from(date).getDayOfWeek(); return dow == SATURDAY ? date.minus(1, DAYS) : dow == SUNDAY ? date.minus(2, DAYS) : date; }).

items.q: Q10. What does 'java.time types are immutable' mean and why does it matter?
items.a: Immutability means no java.time object can be modified after creation. Methods like plusDays(), withMonth(), minusHours() do NOT change the original — they return a NEW object. Example: LocalDate original = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1); original.plusDays(10); System.out.println(original); — prints 2026-01-01, not 2026-01-11! The result of plusDays(10) was discarded. Why it matters: (1) Thread safety — immutable objects are automatically safe to share across threads. (2) No defensive copies needed — you can pass a LocalDate to any method knowing it won't be modified. (3) Predictable behaviour — no unexpected mutations through shared references. Contrast with java.util.Date — setTime() mutates the object, causing thread-safety nightmares.

Java's LocalDate handles this edge case automatically — it adjusts to the last valid day of the resulting month. If 2026 were a leap year, it would give 2026-02-29. This is one of the most important java.time behaviours: it never creates an invalid date by silently overflowing into the next month (unlike Calendar which would give March 3 for calender.add(MONTH, 1) on Jan 31 in some implementations).

Bug: SimpleDateFormat is stateful and NOT thread-safe. Storing it as a static field means multiple threads calling formatDate() concurrently will corrupt each other's formatting state — producing wrong output or exceptions. Fix (best): private static final DateTimeFormatter FORMATTER = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd-MMM-yyyy'); public String formatDate(LocalDate date) { return date.format(FORMATTER); } — DateTimeFormatter is immutable and thread-safe. Fix (legacy workaround): create a new SimpleDateFormat() inside the method each time — no sharing, but allocates per call. Fix (ThreadLocal): private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FORMATTER = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat('dd-MMM-yyyy'));

sections.title: Conclusion — Master Dates, Master Production Reliability

blocks.text: Date and time handling is one of the most underestimated sources of production incidents in enterprise software. Incorrect timezone conversions cause billing on the wrong day. Daylight saving bugs cause missed alerts. Thread-unsafe formatters corrupt financial records. The legacy java.util.Date and Calendar APIs — with their zero-indexed months, mutability, and DST blindness — were responsible for countless production bugs over two decades. java.time eliminates all of these by design.

The hallmark of a production-ready Java developer is using the right type for each temporal concept: LocalDate for date-only data, Instant for machine timestamps, ZonedDateTime for human-facing cross-timezone events, Period for calendar-aware spans, and DateTimeFormatter (never SimpleDateFormat) for all formatting needs.

Your next step: Java Exceptions — where you'll learn how to handle the errors that arise when date parsing fails, invalid dates are constructed, or timezone operations throw unexpected exceptions. Robust error handling around date operations is the final piece of production-ready date/time code. ☕

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Date & Time

items.q: What is the difference between LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime in Java?
items.a: LocalDate stores only date (year-month-day) — perfect for birthdays, holidays, deadlines. LocalDateTime stores date and time but no time zone — ideal for single-zone scheduling and database timestamps where zone is implicit. ZonedDateTime stores date, time, and time zone — required for cross-timezone events, flight schedules, and any globally visible moment. Design principle: use the simplest type that accurately models your data. Unnecessary zone info adds complexity; missing zone info when needed causes silent bugs.

items.q: What is wrong with java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar?
items.a: java.util.Date: mutable (not thread-safe), January = 0 (off-by-one month bugs), getYear() returns year-1900, represents both date and time despite its name, no time zone support, most methods deprecated. java.util.Calendar: still mutable, still 0-indexed months, extremely verbose API, no thread safety. Both are replaced by java.time (Java 8+). SimpleDateFormat — the formatter used with them — is also not thread-safe. Use DateTimeFormatter from java.time.format in all new code.

items.q: What is Instant in Java?
items.a: Instant represents a specific point on the global timeline — nanoseconds elapsed since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC). It is always UTC, has no time zone, and is the most precise and unambiguous temporal type. Use Instant for: database created_at/updated_at columns, event timestamps, JWT token times, measuring elapsed durations, and logging. Convert to ZonedDateTime for human display: instant.atZone(ZoneId.of('Asia/Kolkata')).

items.q: What is the difference between Duration and Period in Java?
items.a: Duration measures time in machine units — seconds and nanoseconds — and is exact: Duration.ofDays(1) is always 86,400 seconds. Use with Instant, LocalTime, LocalDateTime. Period measures time in calendar units — years, months, days — and is human-intuitive: Period.ofMonths(1) added to January 31 gives February 28. Use with LocalDate. Critical DST trap: adding Duration.ofDays(1) to a ZonedDateTime may give 23 or 25 hours on DST transition days; Period.ofDays(1) gives 'same clock time tomorrow'.

items.q: How do you format a date in Java?
items.a: Use DateTimeFormatter from java.time.format — it is thread-safe, immutable, and can be stored as static final. Two approaches: (1) Predefined: DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE for '2026-08-15'. (2) Custom pattern: DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern('dd-MMM-yyyy') for '15-Aug-2026'. Formatting: String s = localDate.format(formatter). Parsing: LocalDate d = LocalDate.parse('15-Aug-2026', formatter). Never use SimpleDateFormat in new code — it is not thread-safe and causes concurrent output corruption when shared across threads.
